label: lem:antiderivatives_diff_constant
title: Two antiderivatives differ by a constant
statement: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $F, G$ both be antiderivatives of $f$ on $(a,b)$ that are continuous on $[a,b]$. Then $F - G$ is constant on $[a,b]$, i.e., for all $x \in [a,b]$, $(F - G)(x) = (F - G)(a)$.
proof: Since $F$ and $G$ are both antiderivatives of $f$ on $(a,b)$, for every $x \in (a,b)$ we have $\texttt{HasDerivAt}\; F\; (f\;x)\; x$ and $\texttt{HasDerivAt}\; G\; (f\;x)\; x$. By the linearity of derivatives, $F - G$ has derivative $f(x) - f(x) = 0$ at every $x \in (a,b)$. Moreover, $F - G$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ since both $F$ and $G$ are. By Lemma~\ref{lem:zero_deriv_constant}, $(F-G)(x) = (F-G)(a)$ for all $x \in [a,b]$.
